en: Having paid homage to the Supreme Lord and then to the sage Bharadvāja,
listen, O you of excellent vows, to the knowledge that has descended from Hara through Indra.
In the meritorious hermitage of Nārāyaṇa, the twice-born Bharadvāja and others performed austerities after installing Śiva there, their minds fixed solely upon him.
Then, perceiving that they had attained spiritual cultivation, the Lord of the Thirty-three once visited their hermitage in person, wearing the garb of an ascetic.
Having been honored by them and having inquired after the well-being of them all, he said:
"For what reason is the dharma of exhortation not followed?"
They said: "O Sage, is this not the Dharma ordained by injunction—a means for propitiating the deities for the attainment of one's desired goals through austerity?"
In the Veda there exists the *raudrī-saṃhitā*, which is to be recited, and Rudra is its deity;
even for the purpose of effecting his presence, the ritual procedure prescribed in the Kalpa is enjoined. (MṛgT 1.1.6)
Even when this was said, the Lord, desiring to know their ultimate disposition, laughed and said to them: "Your knowledge is false; for a deity is a mere word. (MṛgT 1.1.7)
Since it is other than sound, it cannot reach proximity with multiple sacrificers situated simultaneously in different locations; because it possesses form, like ourselves and others. (MṛgT 1.1.8)
And no valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) appears that establishes this without being sublated;
that statement is established otherwise, for where are worldly sayings authoritative?
Thus, like the ocean swelled by the tide of the words of the powerless,
Śakra could not move their mountain-like intellects due to their weight of essential substance.
The form of a deity is never like the bodies of those such as ourselves;
since it is endowed with distinguished sovereignty, this [human body] is not an appropriate illustration for it.
Now, let it be granted that this logic applies to the pot, like the word "Indra" [denoting a jar] because of its being a word;
yet the word "pot" does not take up water, nor does the word "moon" shine. (MṛgT 1.1.12)
Alternatively, let there be another sentence denoting Śakra and so forth;
how then could words such as "action," "form," and so on possess meaningfulness?
Even every popular rumor is false and lacks logical consistency because it has no root;
for if this [world] were rootless, all activities of living beings would be destroyed.
Upon seeing Hara, the sage Upamanyu became free from anger;
how could his word be false, he whose very command the ocean obeys?
Seized by the serpent-noose that emits garlands of poisonous flames,
Śveta was seen by the people with their wealth as he was released by his husband with a roar of "Hūṃ."
Seeing them thus delighted by the praise of Hara during the course of their discourse, with voices choked with tears, Hari became filled with joy.
The god Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt and performer of a hundred sacrifices, revealed his own form,
resembling the rising sun and being praised by the hosts of Maruts.
Bowing down, they praised him with Ṛg verses, Yajus formulas, and Sāman chants.
He said: "Let whatever desire be expressed, even that which is most excellent among all beings."
They chose the auspicious knowledge [of Śiva], saying, "Let it be heard!
He replied, "However, let there be one questioner for me, who is approved by all the listeners. (Mṛgendra-tantra 1.1.20)
Then, among them, the venerable Bharadvāja, the leader,
eloquent and bold, questioned the one honored by the gods in accordance with logic.
How did this supreme knowledge come from Maheśvara? And upon establishing what in his mind did the Blessed One fashion this?
At the time of creation, Maheśāna, for the sake of accomplishing the goals of human existence,
ordains pure knowledge characterized by five streams.
One should contemplate the eight Great Lords who are the objects denoted by the multitude of words residing therein,
as well as the mantras numbering seventy million, within the supreme path.
Furthermore, another [scripture] consisting of eighteen [thousand verses] has been heard, concerning those presiding over *māyā*,
the lords of mantras (*mantreśvara*s), whose splendor is equal to that of the Lord situated on the upper path.
Among those who are fit for accomplishment, that Blessed One becomes manifest and reveals this [teaching] to them; therefore, he reveals whatever meaning is appropriate for others as well.
This knowledge, vomited forth by Śiva, has been proclaimed at great length by the lords of the lords of mantras as the *Kāmika*, because it grants all desires.
Having learned [the truth] from them, the Lord of Umā— whose tree of passion was licked by the flames of the light of his vision—
bestowed upon me [the hymn] in thousands equal in number to Bhava himself.
There too, omitting the detailed accounts, I shall explain the unconfused knowledge primarily by means of those very sūtras that express the essential meaning. (MṛgT 1.29)
Then Śiva, free from beginningless impurity, the doer of all and the knower of all,
removes the net of bonds from the individual soul (aṇu) who was previously bound by it.
The Lord of the World, having condensed the Great Tantra— which consists of three subjects and four feet—
into a single aphorism, spoke it again in detail.
The birth, maintenance, destruction, concealment, and liberation of the world—this alone, along with its instruments and fruits, is to be known as His very activity. (MṛgT 1.2.3)
Therefore, the creator of the world must be established by way of intrinsic nature;
otherwise, if he were established through something posterior, there would be an infinite regress, or liberation would be without cause.
Consciousness, whose nature consists of vision and action, exists in the Self at all times and in every respect;
for it is heard [in scripture] that in liberation it is "facing in all directions" (sarvatomukha).
Even though it exists, because it does not appear, it is perceived as ceased;
for one whose vigor is unobstructed, it is subject [to his will], precisely because it is not released [from that state].
The fourfold activity of Māyā—consisting of *prātibha*, *aiśa*, *bala*, and *karma*—is, in brief, the net of bonds (*pāśajāla*); these phenomena are designated by their very names.
Thus, the application of these three subjects, established in the preceding chapter,
will be explained through the chapters on Conduct, Yoga, and Action.
The fruit of application is liberation, while enjoyment follows as a secondary consequence;
these two are divided into many kinds according to the distinction between the higher and the lower.
In the systems of the Vedānta, Sāṃkhya, and those who maintain the categories of existence and non-existence, liberation exists along with its means; what, then, is the distinction in the Śiva-āgama?
Because the author is all-seeing, the summary of the subject matter is not obscure;
likewise, in Śaivism, these means along with their fruits are all supreme.
"In the Vedāntas, there is only one Self, characterized by conscious and unconscious manifestations"—this is merely a proposition; on what basis is this certainty founded? (MṛgT 1.2.12)
Now, if the self is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) therein, it attains the status of the object of cognition (prameya).
Wherever these two exist, all four [categories] are established there.
In this way, there would be the loss of non-duality; otherwise, it would be devoid of any means of valid cognition.
Furthermore, there would be equality of experience and lack of liberation—two things which are not desired by proponents of the self.
Even in the knowledge of Sāṃkhya, there is falsity, because of the notion of a cause in what is an effect,
because of the non-agency of the enjoyer, and because of [the soul's] independence despite its lack of consciousness.
In this system, there are seven categories: the three consisting of the soul (jīva), the non-soul (ajīva), and influx (āsrava);
as well as restraint (saṃvara), dissociation (nirjarā), and both bondage (bandha) and liberation (mokṣa).

And all these [entities] are marked by the doctrine of manifoldness (syādvāda) because they are non-absolute; for by what means could it be established that "this very thing exists" and "this very thing does not exist"? 1.2.17.

If it were other than existent and other than non-existent, then there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established; for the wise also say that the non-existent is inferior and the existent is superior. MṛgT 1.2.18.
Because of that dependence, both [existence and non-existence] are established in one and the same place;
therefore, if the state of being both existent and non-existent is considered, it is more logical [to say] it is always [both].
And they [the Sāṃkhyas] maintain that it lacks pervasiveness due to the fear of confusion regarding those actions;
for the insentient [pradhāna] lacks the knowledge of its connection with both the universal and the particular.
How could that which was previously non-pervasive become otherwise at the end?
If it possesses properties such as expansion and so forth, then there follows a succession of faults.
Through the thorough knowledge of the six categories, false cognition ceases;
from that [cessation], attachment, aversion, and the sense of "mine"—which are its specific qualities—likewise disappear.
Since those [qualities] born from contact with the body gradually cease, that liberation is of the nature of insentience; therefore, is the liberated one not a corpse? (MṛgT 1.2.23)
Because the karma and other factors that manifest consciousness are momentary, it is manifested again and again;
thus, [consciousness] is considered by others to be momentary as soon as it arises.
Therefore, because of the experience of that non-existent action, there is the recollection of past experience;
for if there were destruction without a causal continuity (*niranvaya*), there would be neither recollection nor [the persistence of] the action. (MṛgT 1.2.25)
The characteristic of destruction departs, yet even in liberation there is no affliction;
nor is there any experience whatsoever [of such a state], therefore the state of worldly existence is better than that.
Relying on such views held by those deluded by ignorance, the dull-witted desire to attain liberation from [the self], like fireflies seeking the light of a fire. (MṛgT 1.2.27)

Whether it be that isolation which arises from the discrimination between the Spirit and Nature, or that cessation which comes from realizing "all is Brahman," or whatever other liberations are born of bonds— on creation, they all return to differentiation.
Established in Śiva, he shines at the summit above all others; liberated, he does not descend again into creation.
Having supported all things with his own abode, he remains forever as the Lord of all lords.
Then, having apprehended the body and other such entities as possessing the property of being effects,
we know their agent through inference as one who is distinguished [by specific qualities].
Even in the established order of the world, excellence [of the cause] is observed from the excellence of the effect.
In Trilocana’s *Siddhāntārthasamuccaya* (IFP MS T.206, p. 62 and T.284, p. 133):
"In whatever manner, in whatever form, and to whatever extent an effect exists, its cause is likewise.
Being eternal due to not being delimited by time, and because it lacks spatial extension, it does not occupy a specific location. (MṛgT 1.3.2)

Because production occurs both successively and non-successively, that which possesses the power to produce in succession and so forth must have an instrument, for no action is observed to be without an instrument.
And that [cause] should be known as non-returning (anāgāmi), because the effect is established from beginningless time;
nor is the instrument anything other than power, and power is not insentient, for it is consciousness.
Because there is no restriction regarding their objects, consciousness is one;
likewise, its function is such that it does not produce effects such as persistence or birth for the seed, primordial matter, or the atom.
By process of elimination, that [object] is indeed Śiva, the liberated Maheśvara;
for no one encounters any sublation of their cognition when the relationship [between the word and its referent] is not grasped. (MṛgT 1.3.6)
Moreover, smoke on a mountain is seen by people in the world to be different from that produced in a kitchen and the like; it is observed to have a physical form, just like that of us and others.
Because the [five] roots and so forth are impossible, the body of the Lord is not of such a nature;
rather, that body consists of five mantras which are applicable to the fivefold activity (pañcakṛtya). (Mṛgendratantra 1.3.8)
The head and other parts [of the body] are associated with Īśa, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāma, and Jyeṣṭha, by means of which supreme quality He rules over the entire universe. (Mṛgendratantra 1.3.9)
Because it is at the level of the head, it is called "mūrdhan," though it is not a limb of the body;
for it devours that particular body by means of which it exists within it.
In that regard, because of protection (*tatrāṇa*) and manifestation (*vyañjana*), he has the face of that Puruṣa;
"heart" (*hṛdaya*) is a synonym for awakening (*bodha*), since Śiva is his Aghora. (MṛgT 1.3.11)
Because its grasping is terrible, it is called "terrible" by way of metaphor;
because it is opposed to the three aims of life (trivarga), it is "left" (vāma); and because it is secret by its very nature, it is "secret" (guhya). He whose supreme abode is secret is Vāmaguhyaka.
Because he brings about the forms of atoms instantly by his will, he is designated as "Sadya" (the Immediate);
or because he instantly bestows forms upon yogins, he is called "Sadyomūrti" (of Immediate Form), due to the swiftness of his action and not because of a physical body.
Thus, while performing the functions of the body, Śakti is designated by the terms "body" due to the absence of [any other] body;
and even those divisions of hers, such as Vāmā and the rest, are likewise described by the wise according to the distinction of their functions.
With such a body and with this instrument whose vigor has been struck down,
he always performs whatever task is appropriate at any given time.
Therein, at the outset, he creates an eightfold group of pure, qualified atoms,
joined with the powers beginning with Vāmā and accompanied by a retinue of seventy million.
Of them, Ananta, Sūkṣma, and likewise Śivottama,
Ekanetra, Ekarudra, Trimūrti, and Amitadyuti [are the lords].
Śrīkaṇṭha and Śikhaṇḍin, who are the lords of the lords of the kings of kings,
are to be appointed by Parameṣṭhin because they have not yet fully attained yoga.
Even though they possess qualities such as omniscience, they remain subject to application due to a portion of impurity;
thus, the mantras situated below are distinguished from one another.
And impelled by the power of Śiva manifested as the Lord of Mantras,
they bestow grace upon those men with whom He is united when the time is right.
Having performed its office throughout the entire path— depending on the body of the practitioner for half of it—
it enters into Śiva along with the Lord at the end of its duration.
Apart from the substratum, another [power] belonging to the primary transformation,
having performed its desired office for the Lord, departs at the time of the withdrawal of its own path.
Then, manifested from Ananta and the others through the principle of the knots (granthi-tattva) of the Lords,
[Ananta] brings about one hundred and eighteen [deities] for those whose bodies have begun with the limited power (kalā) and so forth.
The Blessed One, having entered even those world-lords who possess eyes—those from whom all this [universe] proceeds and whose power is bound by karma—[acted]. (MṛgT 1.4.10)
The authors of the treatises on sacrificial animals, the animals that follow those [treatises],
and those endowed with the instruments for their own goals, all exist until the end of the abode of Time.
In the state of persistence, having overtaken these [beings] along with their causal instruments by means of his own splendor,
he joins them to the accomplishment of his own purpose, unobserved by the beings themselves.
Having projected the means of enjoyment and having established the causal substratum,
it then seizes that [substratum] along with the self and remains for the sake of rest.
Because he is devoted to the welfare of all beings, [the Lord], having reached the end of his sleep for those who are subject to existence and weary of cyclic existence, proceeds once more as before.
Even while in sleep, He remains awake, awakening those capable of being awakened and restraining those who must be restrained;
He brings to fruition the karma of the bound souls, making manifest His powers of illusion (māyā-śakti) that are ready for manifestation, perceiving every category of reality exactly as it is.

Upon the cessation of the dominance of the power of tamas and the soul's liberation from it, Śiva reveals the infinity of knowledge and action to that individual soul, who is the ornament of the universe.
Those whom she liberates in sleep immediately become auspicious;
whether in the state of withdrawal or emergence, they become either individual souls (aṇavas) or lords (patayas).
Those who possess consciousness become partakers of the state of Īśāna, the Lord of the Rudra-mantras,
when they rely upon a Guru and are graced by him during their worldly existence.
For those embodied beings whose power falls even toward cessation,
their indicative mark is a longing for liberation and an aversion to remaining in worldly existence.
Devotion toward the devotees of Śiva and faith in the rule that governs them— by this,
even those of dull intellect can infer the cause of the learned (the Śiṣṭas).
For those who perceive like animals and for those perfected through yoga, the two manifestations of karma are equal;
likewise for those fit for fruits such as the "eldest" state, in regard to liberations that involve further qualification.
Furthermore, due to the distinction of the specific methods employed, those three are sought again;
among the two, there is a certain [method] that brings about manifestation, characterized by the attainment of either transcendence or supernatural powers.
When the obstructive power of the Lord of Darkness has ceased by half, or when it remains slightly residual,
these signs appear for embodied beings.
Having transcended even these three types of fitness, Maheśvara favors [the soul] during its state of sleep, because this [state] possesses the capacity for further spiritual authority.

At the root of creation, on the third [day], as in the dissolution of beings, that which is performed after setting aside [the gross body] like sleep— that which is of such a nature is called the *aṇu* (the individual soul).
In the same way, the seed of the body and so forth ripens until the time of entry [into the womb];
it does not immediately become a factor for suitability, just like medicinal herbs and the like.
Even though it is capable of being cooked, it cannot cook itself by itself;
this is the common nature of all things that are subject to transformation.

The omniscient one is so because he is the creator of all; it is well-established that whoever knows something and performs it, he alone accomplishes that very thing, along with the means, the constituent parts, and the results.
And because it is devoid of obscuration, it does not depend upon a manifestor;
therefore, it is never subject to doubt, nor is it ever otherwise.
Those [powers] which perceive the manifestor because they are enveloped by the powers of impurity may,
in accordance with that manifestor, appear to be obstructed as well.
The stainless knowledge of Śaṅkara does not appear as perceptual, nor as inferential, nor even as verbal,
yet it shines eternally regarding all things.
That single [consciousness], due to the infinity of its objects, undergoes an infinity of distinctions;
because it is non-different from that [object], agency likewise follows through metaphorical attribution.

Those who know the reality of the Lord through insights that are directed toward the purpose of realizing the nature of the seven categories—even when those insights have arisen only in a fragmentary way—they liberate living beings submerged in the mire of worldly existence; they do not [liberate them] by means of men who are themselves bound by the fetters of *paśu*. 1.5.18.
Now, although the definition of the Self as the cause of all has for the most part been established by the Lord’s own statement,
it is nevertheless stated here by way of brief enumeration.

Earth and the other elements are the effect; God is the agent. That agent is not required for the sake of that [effect], because it is insentient and thus has no purpose of its own, nor is there any lack of purpose, since the agent is exalted.
By process of elimination, that [body] exists for the sake of another; he is the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), the Supreme among those two.
Since the body is for his sake, the earth and other elements are indeed for the sake of another. 1.6.3.
The body, too, because it lacks consciousness, more easily serves another's purpose;
for if it were conscious, it would never be an object of enjoyment due to its being subject to modification.
Objects such as cloth and the like are seen to be objects of experience, subject to change, and devoid of consciousness;
furthermore, consciousness does not exist either when that [body] is present or even when it is absent, as in the case of a corpse.
If it is argued that memory does not exist because of the specific nature of transformation (*pariṇāma*), that is not so;
for such [transformation] is well-established, and therefore there exists a rememberer other than the body.
He is neither non-pervasive, nor momentary, nor manifold, nor insentient in nature;
he is not a non-agent, for once the bonds have ceased, he attains the state of Śiva through the union with distinct consciousness.
Now, the fetters beginning with ignorance (avidyā) are briefly described here,
by the removal of which the individual souls (aṇu) become lords of the world.
In the absence of bonds, what basis could there be for speaking of dependence on another?
If it were inherent, then the term "liberated" would cease to apply to those who are liberated.
Mastery belongs to one who is free from bondage, while subjection belongs to one who is bound;
such is the extent of bondage and liberation for those who are bound and those who are liberated.
Bondage is dependence upon that [other]; since that [Self] is eternal, like consciousness and so forth, the entire collection of means for liberation is useless—enough with this line of thought.

Even though he is a treasury of the eternal, all-pervading power of consciousness, he does not seek any other strength— whether it be the power of the fettered (pāśava) or that of Śambhu (śāmbhava)— unless it is for the sake of accomplishing a specific purpose.
That obscuration of this individual soul (aṇu) within the fivefold stream of Śiva is sung of by many synonymous terms; it is always unseen by those bound in ignorance (paśus).
By means of the mist of animal-nature, the darkness of death, the impurity of fainting,
the veil of ignorance, the sickness of exhaustion, and the destruction of the root of sin, and so forth.
That [Self] is one, the beginningless, dense, and great essence of all beings; it possesses a multitude of powers that abide within each individual soul and persist until the end of its own time.

If it is argued that this [obstruction] exists from beginningless time or arises subsequently as its cause, and that it obstructs only those who are not liberated—then effort toward liberation would be in vain. (MṛgT 1.7.9)
That [Self] is indeed one, yet it appears as many because it possesses such a nature of origination;
however, its powers are manifold, since simultaneous liberation is not observed.
Among them, the power of Maheśvara is Śivā, who bestows grace upon all;
yet, precisely because she follows after dharma, she is metaphorically designated as "bond" (pāśa).

And when it transforms these [objects] up to the limit of obstruction by means of its own radiant consciousness, and brings about their manifestation, then it is called "gracious" (anugrāhikā). (MṛgT 1.7.12)
Since that which is to be graced by Śambhu through consciousness and so forth is mutually contradictory, it is not possible for them to exist simultaneously;
how then can His power be one that bestows grace upon all?
How is it appropriate for the Lord of the World, who has engaged in activity for the sake of benefiting living beings,
to enter into one who causes harm and subject him to piercing pain?
It does not grant favor to even the slightest impurity for the sake of tormenting it;
rather, whatever is done is performed by means of an expedient, and not otherwise.
Liberation does not occur for anyone while there is still a governing authority within darkness;
even that authority ceases through the transformation of its own power.
Even that [activity] would not arise from itself alone,
because an insentient thing, even when capable, must always and in every way be employed by consciousness.

Just as a physician, even while causing pain with caustic substances and the like, is not perceived as a cause of suffering because he bestows the desired goal upon the patient, so too [is the teacher]. (MṛgT 1.7.18)
Because the Great Lord is omnipresent, his presiding power is never obstructed;
nor does he remain indifferent toward that which requires his action.
What is called "favoring the possessor" (dharmin) is simply following that which belongs to him;
there is no one at all who does not ever follow their husband.
For one whose frost of excessive exertion has passed away, there prospers the favor toward another being;
for that [other] is the purpose of his action.

The persistence of the two qualities of being the knower and being transformed, and the cessation of the defilement along with its governing authority upon the relinquishing of that [state]. MṛgT 1.7.22.

Thus, whether simultaneously or sequentially, that very [state] is indeed well-established for Māyā while she still possesses her authority, and it has been declared to be the same for Karma as well. (MṛgT 1.7.23)

Now, the conjunction of consciousness [with matter] is inferred by means of the sense organs, the body, and their objects; for it has a cause, since that which is not yet arisen cannot be without a cause. (MṛgT 1.8.1)
Because it exists in specific locations, because of its diversity, because of its momentariness,
because it is restricted to each individual, and because it is continuous, it possesses those qualities.

Because it depends on the knowledge of Īśa and other factors, karma is called a "cooperative cause" (sahakārin); because it is produced by an activity, it is called "unseen" (adṛṣṭa) due to its subtle nature.
It is the producer, the sustainer, and the object of enjoyment; it is the threefold means consisting of the internal [self] and so forth;
and because it is the source of both truth and falsehood, its nature consists of dharma and adharma.
During [the Lord's] sleep, it undergoes maturation; at the time of his creation, it is employed;
it persists within the power of illusion (māyā) until the end, and that which has not been experienced does not go to dissolution.
Thus, this beginningless karma, which sets in motion everything from illusion (māyā) up to time (kāla), is a manifestor; yet, because it is obstructive, it does not lead to immediate liberation.
Now, the characteristic of that which is understood through the word of the Omniscient One—
the knot and the snare— is described slightly, by way of reasoning and in brief.
That single, inauspicious seed of the world possesses manifold powers;
it obstructs the end of the period of its auxiliary conditions, is all-pervasive, and is imperishable.
By whatever causal property of the world the agent is inferred, by that same [property] the material cause also exists; for there is no cloth without threads.
That [cause] must indeed be insentient, because the effect is observed to be insentient;
otherwise, the fault of the lack of causal necessity would follow, resulting in the loss of all [causal order].
If this effect is impermanent, why does it arise again?
And if it were non-pervasive, how could it be present for all [beings] in every direction?
That which is observed to have multiple mental states and to possess the property of arising does not [itself] arise; therefore, let it be accepted as one.
A cloth is seen to arise from a multitude of threads; thus, the one arises from the many. Yet even that multiplicity is produced from a single seed.
For those according to whom even a non-sentient thing arises from a cause that is sentient,
why is water not inferred by means of the mark of smoke?
For those for whom atoms are the ultimate cause of the world, reaching its very limit,
the subtlety of their knowledge is indeed understood from the reason previously stated.

If the body and so forth were produced from the body and so forth, then what would happen when all of those [causes] perish? There would be no total destruction, and one who is not omniscient would not speak falsely.
If a property is perceived even in one part of a given subject,
by what means can its occurrence throughout that entire subject be prevented?
Having witnessed the deaths of embodied beings by the millions as they gather together,
one also perceives that time in which there is the destruction of all people without exception.
In the state of withdrawal, the effects that have that [power] as their support exist in the form of potentiality;
in the state of manifestation, they function in the form of actualization for the accomplishment of purposes.
For one who desires a cloth, the taking up of causal factors such as the threads would be pointless if the cloth were non-existent;
yet if it were existent, even the word "causal factor" would cease to apply—thus, the entire world is ruined.
Let there be success for the causal entity in the production of what is non-existent;
let everything produce from everything whatever is desired.
Now, since that which is impossible [cannot be established], what is it for you that serves as the regulator here?
I do not see any such thing; if it were a capacity, then you would be proving what is already established.

Otherwise, because the activity of the multitude of causal factors would be untenable, the scriptural injunction for taking [the fire], as well as its purpose, would be lost; thus that [position] is also refuted.
Now, if there exists a power that produces [an effect], but the effect is not of the nature of that power, then a distinction between the two must be stated; yet I do not see any such thing at all.
Therefore, the generative power of the causal entity is that which determines [the effect];
it is ascertained either through positive and negative concomitance or by conventional usage.
The manifestation of that [effect] is called "production" (janana), because it depends upon its causes;
by means of this, the form residing in the threads is subsumed within the form of the cloth.

Just as the manifestation of a cloth hidden by a mat or similar object is revealed by removing that [obscuring] thing, so too the manifestation of the [individual soul], which was bound by the *kalās* and other factors, is not produced from non-existence, but is revealed by their removal. (MṛgT 1.9.21)

Born from the knot [of Māyā] are, in sequence, Kalā, Kāla, Vidyā, Rāga, Niyati, and Puruṣa; then the Guṇas, Buddhi, Ahaṃkāra, Cittam, the Indriyas, the Tanmātras, and the Bhūtas. (Mṛgendratantra 1.10.1)
That which directly ordains [the means] for the sake of achieving the body, from which other states arise,
and how it joins [the soul] and for what purpose— it is that very thing which is now described.
The agentive power of the individual soul is eternal and all-pervasive, like the power of the Lord;
yet, being obscured by darkness, it does not shine forth with respect to objects unless it is accompanied by grace.

Hara, having agitated Māyā, creates that supreme reality called Kalā, which is luminous (taijasa) and supportive of that [limited subjectivity], for it is indeed the primary factor for worldly activity.
By means of that [knowledge] which is like a lamp, the atom of non-lucid consciousness illuminates one portion [of its object], having torn asunder the dense darkness.
The verbal root *kal* signifies both numbering and impelling; that *kalā* (digit/aspect) is so called because it performs the impelling that drives away darkness. MṛgT 1.10.6.
O Brahmin, these two, existing together as if they were non-different,
constitute the agent and the instrument for a living being in the performance of the act of enjoyment.
Thus, one whose power of action has become manifest, desiring the object of sight,
resorts to that which requires grace, being unable to see by himself.
For that purpose, the Lord, having agitated Kalā alone which is capable of generating,
created the principle called Vidyā, the instrument of the Supreme Self.
By means of that luminous form which impels the power of cognition,
it perceives the supreme object to be accomplished by all the causal factors.
Even one who has seen the object through the power of consciousness manifested by that [pleasure] remains free from thirst;
he does not develop that passion which produces rebirth. Therefore, the Lord created that very [pleasure].
Delighted by that, he longs for even defiled objects of enjoyment;
yet, while enjoying them, he does not attain detachment.
Thus engaged through the instruments (karaṇas) that have ascended to the state of effects and are associated with the worlds,
the person (nā) experiences enjoyments in the lands of enjoyment (bhogabhūmis) in accordance with time.

Time is the object of cognitions such as the *tuṭi* and so forth; it arises from *māyā*, and by means of *niyati*, it impels the bound soul (*paśu*) toward its emergence, determining [its state] through the process of *kalana*.
Some have declared that since enjoyment together with its means is dependent upon karma, it is karma—nothing other than that—which acts as the regulator. (MṛgT 1.10.15)
The object of experience is the purpose of all principles, and that too is bound by karma;
let karma alone then be the body and so forth—therefore, everything else is useless.
Now, if that [karma] which accomplishes the goals of man depends upon the body and so forth,
then let karma be the regulator, depending upon *niyati* (destiny).
From that very [source], the principle of the person (puṃstattva) arose,
which is the basis for the cognition of "person," which fills the primary matter (pradhāna) and the rest, and which rests upon Rudra, the lord of the elemental beings (bhauvana).
Then the principle of Pradhāna was produced from the principle of Kalā;
it is the cause of that which is secondary, being the source of the seven knots.
Therefore, the primary material cause of intellect and the rest is the secondary [form of] *sattva*, along with *rajas* and *tamas*;
their functions, such as illumination and so forth, are indeed well known for the most part.
"Nevertheless, although there are three qualities (guṇas), that reality (tattva) is one because they are inseparable;
the singular designation for each of these is based on the predominance of their respective functions."
There is no insentient thing whatsoever in this world that is not pervaded by the qualities (guṇas), nor is there any in which even a single quality is unmixed.
Beyond that is the principle of intellect (buddhitattva), characterized by the various cognitions of objects;
it is the supreme object of experience for the self, refined by the meanings to be described hereafter.

The states consisting of the qualities of the intellect—namely, virtue, knowledge, dispassion, and power—are of the nature of *sattva*; when these are reversed and devoid of passion (*rāga*), they become of the nature of *tamas*.

O Sage, those conditions and their respective substrates are renowned as eight and nine, each possessing four qualities; likewise, the [powers] beginning with *siddhi* are declared in groups of seven and five. MṛgT 1.10.25.
Entities possess causal conditions; their characteristics are stated here briefly. These belong to the atom (aṇu) and are of three kinds: innate, acquired through discipline, and natural.
For those whose minds are illuminated by the impressions of distinguished dharmas,
their innate quality shines forth even in the absence of a body, just as before.
The quality of being disciplined shines forth from the world, the mind, and the scriptures;
the state of being disciplined is acquired through the activities of mind, speech, and body.
In the state of Prakṛti, when there is conjunction with the body, [the soul] becomes manifest, like the cognition of dreams and so forth;

heaven, liberation, the absence of obstruction, transcendence of the womb, the attainment of hell, and bondage—all these objects of purpose regarding forms that are both refined and natural—come to fruition in succession, accompanied by obstructions. (MṛgT 1.10.29)
Subjugation, mastery, the yoga of thorough knowledge thereof, lack of desire for enjoyments, the removal of the host of obstacles,
attachment to enjoyments, humiliation, the attainment of a body, and obstacles regarding wealth— these are the [eight] accomplishments among those that are spontaneously perfected.
Now, the general definition of the groups beginning with the Siddhas is stated in brief, so that there may be no confusion arising from their detailed classification.
The cognition whose objects are the Puruṣa, Prakṛti, and so forth, is what is here called "accomplishment" (siddhi).
Contentment (tuṣṭi), on the other hand, is the thought of one who has not yet achieved his goal: "I have achieved my goal. (MṛgT 1.11.2)
Incapacity is the inability to produce a real object due to the deficiency of causal factors;
it is a certain cognition based on a general similarity [with another object], while a different cognition [arising] elsewhere is error.
The establishment of manifestation and the like as being illuminating arises from the nature of sattva;
furthermore, because it is directed toward the purpose of illumination, it also originates from a portion of rajas.

O Brahmin, contentment, because its nature is false, is rooted in the quality of darkness (tamas); yet, because it takes the form of pleasure, it is also perceived as belonging to the quality of goodness (sattva).

Incapacity is characterized by a lack of activity and belongs to the quality of darkness (tamas) because it consists of suffering; however, even in that which belongs to the quality of passion (rajas), a quality is observed in the effect based upon its cause.
Its opposite is the womb of darkness, and it is characterized by a false form;
because it appears as a mere generality, it is determined to be the self of a sentient being.
Thus, this manifestation of the intellect, characterized by the suffix denoting abstract state (*bhāvapratyaya*),
is called "awakening" (*bodha*) because it serves as the ground for the manifestation of awakening in the bound soul (*paśu*).
If consciousness is the cause of cognition, then knowledge is distinct from it;
likewise, even if passion is absent, what can attachment—which is the source of the creative powers—accomplish?
If, when another manifestor exists, the manifestor were purposeless,
then even when the mind, the deity, and the object exist, cognition would likewise be purposeless.
Now, some might say this with the intention of [the mind] being an instrument;
however, that position too is considered inconclusive by those who maintain that the mind is the sixth among the senses.
Now, if there were only a single function, then one [organ] would be redundant;
therefore, let the ear, eye, hand, foot, and so forth have distinct objects for the person.
Furthermore, there is no way for knowledge and cognition to have a single function;
nor is it faulty for them to have multiple effects through different modes of application.

Vidyā is the manifest power of the individual consciousness; impelled by the Lord of the senses, it takes as its objects those things within the range of the senses, and brings about the state of being an object for the instruments employed by the person.

Attachment is not something other than the cognition of the object, nor is it secondary, because it possesses properties contrary to that [cognition]; and since that [attachment] consists either in the state of being an object of enjoyment or in this very [cognition], one who is free from attachment would consequently be destroyed.
Desire is that longing for objects which does not exist in the two [other] types of objects;
let karma be postulated as the pervasive factor, since it exists even in the case of the other imagined [object].
It has been stated that the refutation applies only to the case of karma acting alone under the principle of necessity;
there is no fault of non-coexistence [between karma and the afflictions], because hatred and attachment are not identical.
The activity of everyone at all times arises from the notion of pleasure;
for one who is thus engaged, pleasure, pain, or even delusion subsequently arise.
Following engagement comes aversion, and passion precedes it;
at the end of aversion, there is that [passion] again, which is the cause for the application of vigor.
Then, from the manifestation of another [principle], pride (garva) arose as an instrument of consciousness;
through its activity, the five bodily winds (vāyus) exert their functions.
Prāṇa, apāna, and the others are indeed distinct only by way of their functions, not in reality. O Bharadvāja, listen as I describe their functions briefly to you. (MṛgT 1.11.21)
The application known as "leading forth" (praṇayana) is called "living" (jīvana);
that which is the deliberation (ūha) of men's minds wanders like one who is blind, searching for the path. (MṛgT 1.11.22)

That which performs this [function] is called *prāṇa*; or rather, it is *prāṇa* by virtue of its connection with the vital breath (*prāṇana*). The word *prāṇa* is applied to the conscious transportive power (*ativāhikī śakti*), as well as to the *kalās*. MṛgT 1.11.23.
Likewise, by performing the removal of what has been eaten, drunk, excrement, urine, and semen,
it is designated as *apāna* by those who perceive the truth.
Because it distributes food and drink equally in all directions, it is called *samāna*; *vyāna* is so named because it pervades and bends the body.
By means of that [unmanifest sound], which is preceded by the intention to speak and effort, and which possesses the quality of the space within the chest,
the state of being a phoneme (varṇatā) is produced with the assistance of the organ of speech.

That udāna [vital breath] resides within this body; its function is the maintenance [of the body], and its fruit is mastery. The remainder of what was to be said has been transferred by the Lord to another section.

Then, for the sake of accomplishing the remaining purposes, he— having attained the power of the Lord— extracted from that very [source] three aggregates (skandhas) which were predominantly characterized by *sattva* and the other [guṇas].

The Taijasa is the Vaikṛta, while the other is traditionally known as the Bhūtādi; from these [two] arise the deities consisting of the subtle elements (mātrās), and from those subtle elements arises the group of five gross elements.
The ear, skin, eyes, tongue, and nose, together with the mind, are characterized by sattva due to their connection with light; that [state] is the taijasa, and it is sattvic.
Speech, hands, the organ of generation, the anus, and the feet—these constitute the group born of rajas;
because it follows from activity, this group here is predominantly rajasic and is of the modified (vaikārika) nature.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth—
these subtle elements (tanmātras), characterized by their specific qualities, are designated by the term "tanmātra."
Because it differs from the group that performs the function of illumination, and because it is itself to be illuminated, the *bhūtādi* ego is of the nature of *tamas*. (MṛgT 1.12.6)
The mind is that which initiates action toward the gods, acts swiftly, and has the nature of volition; the senses, such as hearing and the rest, are the perceivers of objects such as sound.
The functions of speech and the other [senses]— namely speaking, taking, delighting, emitting,
and moving— are distinct from the words [they produce], even though those words exist within them, for they do not possess the qualities of the words.
When there is no proximity between the self, the sense organs, and their objects, there is a total lack of activity;
furthermore, the existence of the factors that cause activity is established even through reasoning.
Because it differs from the functions described for the other principles, volition (saṃkalpa) is distinct; by the process of elimination, it reaches the mind as its seed.
That cognition, due to its connection with the senses, appears sequentially according to the sequence [of the objects];
nevertheless, it appears as if simultaneous because of its rapid movement, were it not for that rapidity.
The sense organs belong to someone [who is a transmigrating soul] because they have fixed objects and arise from various sources;
furthermore, because they manifest odors and so forth, they are also of the nature of their substrates.
The ear grasps sound alone, and the skin grasps touch alone;
let it be so, provided that it does not apprehend another cause along with its qualities.
The sense of touch perceives objects that are not currently in contact [with it] and turns away from those that are;
however, the visual faculty perceives the substances of fire, water, and earth together with their forms.
Consequently, that [cognition] would arise from three substances; however, it is not accepted as such by others.
Whatever object is perceived by whatever means, that [means] is the cause of that object.
Even though karma and the like have not been attained, this continuous succession of calamities arises;
it is like the space within the cavity of the ear, which manifests the range of sounds.

Tell me, by what can that [wind] which is distinguished by the nostrils be obstructed? Or if it is held back by unseen forces (adṛṣṭa), why is that same force not applied elsewhere as well? (MṛgT 1.12.17)
One does not grasp a musical instrument that has been seized by some bandit;
even when a matter is beyond the reach of logical reasoning, conviction arises from the words of the virtuous, yet it remains fraught with peril.
The wise maintain that the immeasurable object is superior to the measurable object.
Space, air, fire, water, and earth constitute the pentad of elements.
Sound and the other [elements] possess one additional quality each, and their functions consist of providing space and so forth;
the qualities [of the elements] are known by their shaking, burning, floating, and hardness.
Sound resides in air and the other elements, as well as in space; it consists of resonance and its reflection.
Furthermore, [the functions of the elements are] structural arrangement, the providing of space, digestion, cohesion, and support.
The functions of air, space, fire, water, and earth [are established], and sound is indeed a quality of space, because it is perceived elsewhere than in those [other elements]. (MṛgT 1.12.22)
Some say, "O Blessed One, how can there be the qualities of all beings?
How could those qualities exist elsewhere than in the space of hearing, and how could they exist elsewhere? (MṛgT 1.12.23)

If you then think that, in that case, human experience is the determiner [of truth] based on another's desired source—even when it occurs right at the root of one's ear—and that this is what constitutes consciousness; MṛgT 1.12.24.
Let its transformation be like that of the auditory faculty; what harm is there?
Reasons contradicted by scripture and perception do not establish the intended object.
The experts in logic know that [the argument] is "mistimed" (kālātyayāpadiṣṭa);
thus it is established that even this odor may be a quality of space (nabhas).

"Since sound is perceived even when there is a separation from [the source], such as a *ketaka* flower, this sound exists in the five [substances], while touch exists in the four elements. (MṛgT 1.12.27)
The wind and earth possess cold and heat; water and fire possess cold and heat;
the sun and fire possess light; water possesses whiteness; and earth possesses whiteness and many other qualities.
Form exists in the three [subtle elements]; taste exists in water and is of six kinds;
odor exists in earth and is considered by the wise to be both unpleasant and pleasant.
In the body, earth is present in the bones, flesh, hair, skin, nails, and teeth;
water is established in the urine, blood, phlegm, sweat, semen, and so forth.
Fire resides in the heart, the digestive organ, and the bile, because its characteristic qualities are observed there;
and the wind, through its various functions such as the vital breath (prāṇa) and so forth, has indeed been described by you [as being present] even in space.

Through the persistence of the state of pride, this subtle means for accomplishing one's purpose extends from the practitioner and so forth to the ends of the earth, pervading the entire void within all the channels.
It is determined to be restricted to each individual according to the distinction of their experience;
because it functions simultaneously with respect to everything, yet does not arise [simultaneously for all], it is not omnipresent.
Even though they belong to different classes, they have a single result, like the various components of a lamp.
Thus, this subtle body (*ātivāhika*) of the living being revolves within the depths of consciousness through its connection with consciousness;

yet, this alone is not sufficient. Therefore, for the sake of the emergence of the foundational body and its objects, I shall describe the series of the principles of the elemental worlds (*bhuvana*).
Then, for the sake of establishing the aforementioned purpose, Maheśvara fashioned the worlds and so forth from the common sources of origin, beginning with *kalā*.
Those [elements], beginning with the fire of time (kālānala) and ending with the subtle divisions (kalā), constitute the mandala;
those who know reality declare this to be saṃsāra, the locus of experience.
In the *Māyā* [tattva] as well, Gahaneśa and others are recited as the presiding deities;
furthermore, the purification of the principles (*tattvaśuddhi*) during initiation—all that is at the head of his composition.
From the scriptural declarations of its eternity, omnipresence, and so forth,
it is determined that the perceptible world, beginning with the city [of Brahmā], which is an object of experience, corporeal, and subject to dissolution, [is not the ultimate reality].
Even in the pure path (śuddhādhvan), the lords of the supreme Māyā are mentioned;
they too are recited at the head of her creation.
Dust is perceived when the rays of the sun enter through a lattice;
at the third stage, which consists of eight times eight qualities, there would be a single hair-tip.
Likewise, a nit (likṣā), a louse (yūkā), and a barleycorn (yava) [are each three times the size of the preceding]; a finger-breadth (aṅgula) consists of those [barleycorns] multiplied by three.
A cubit (pāṇi) is that same [finger-breadth] multiplied by twenty-four, and a bow (dhanus) is marked by four of those.
A *daṇḍa* should be known as two *dhanus*; a *krośa* is two thousand of those;
they say two *krośas* constitute a *gavyūti*, and twice a *gavyūti* is a *yojana*.
The skull [of Brahmā] is called Arbuda because of its vastness, measuring as many yojanas as the Egg of Brahmā;
within it is the golden abode, which is indeed of the same extent as that of the Fire of Time.
There dwells the God renowned as Kālāgni, surrounded by Rudras of such a kind, whose brilliance is like the sharp rays of the sun at the time of universal destruction.
When that [power] of the Lord, impelled by the destructive Śakti, has its energy aroused, fear arises among all beings existing throughout the three times.
From its very nature, ten crores of flames burst forth,
and a thick, most dreadful smoke rose for half that distance in yojanas.
Then there are thirty-three *puṭas*, each measuring nine hundred thousand [yojanas];
the intervals between them are thirty-two hundred thousand [yojanas] for those of evil nature.
O foremost of the twice-born, I shall describe by name those places of torment fashioned by the Ordainer of the world for the sake of retribution; listen to me.
Raurava, Dhvānta, Śīta, Uṣṇa, Saṃtāpa, Abja, Mahāmbuja, and Kālasūtra as the eighth—these are indeed renowned as the hells. (MṛgT 1.13.15)
O Sage, those [hells] known as Sūcyāsya (Needle-mouth), Tālaka (Palm-tree), Khaḍga (Sword), Kṣuradhārā (Razor-edge), Ambarīṣa (Frying-pan),
Kālakhaḍga (Black-sword),
Taptaṅgāra (Heated Coals), Mahādāha (Great Burning), and Saṃtāpa (Torment).
There are eight extremely loathsome [hells], following upon great sounds and words:
Lākṣāpralepa, Māṃsāda, Nirucchvāsa, and Nasocchvāsa.
Yugma, Adri, Śālmalī, Loha, Pradīpta, Kṣutpipāsaka,
and Kṛmīṇāṃnicaya— these are proclaimed as the kings [of the hells].
Then there are the Iron Pillar, excrement and urine, as well as the Vaitaraṇī River,
Tāmisra, Andhatāmisra, Kumbhīpāka, and Raurava.
Mahāpadma, Anūpa, and Avīci are the lords of the lords of the kings of kings;
these hells, together with their respective pits, are measured in yojanas.
O best of the twice-born, there are thirty-two million [yojanas];
then, having subtracted thirty thousand, the earth consists of nine hundred thousand [yojanas].
It consists of half iron and half gold;
furthermore, its lower crucible is half clay and half iron.
There resides the lord of these thirty-two hells,
renowned as Kūṣmāṇḍa, possessing the radiance of the fire of the sun at the end of an aeon.
With a terrifying face, enraged, and with eyes like deep-set hollows,
he held a trident in his hand and was surrounded by many other such beings.
Above the layer of iron and gold is this eighth earth;
six thousand [yojanas] thick, it is the middle one, measuring two hundred ninety-nine million [yojanas].
The Vasatis are nine thousand [yojanas], and the next is ten thousand;
thus, these seven together are known by the wise as the seven Pātālas.
Understand from me that which is called by its name as the sovereign [deity]:
Ābhāsa, Paratālākhya, Tritala, and Gabhastimān.
Mahātala, Rasātala, and Pātāla as the seventh, O Sage—
within these seven [netherworlds] dwell the lords of the Daityas, the serpents, and the night-stalkers.
Seven [groups] have been enumerated; now learn of them from me:
among the Daityas, Śaṅkuśruti was the first, followed by Prahlāda and Śiśupālaka.
Karkandhaka, Hiraṇyākṣa, Bṛhadgarbha, and Bali;
likewise the sons of Kadrū: Kuṭilaka, Vāsuki, and Kambala.
Then Kārkoṭaka, Kālāṅga, Durdarśa, and likewise Takṣaka;
Vikaṭa, Lohitākṣa, Yamākṣa, and Vikaṭānana.
Karāla, Bhīmanirhrāda, and Piṅgala are the Rākṣasas;
above them is the sovereign lord of all the remaining netherworlds (pātālas).
Within the golden mandala of the thousandfold abode, Hāṭaka resides—
he whom those striving for the attainment of their beloved praise with self-restraint and ascetic ornaments.
Then, with graceful steps, the wives of the lords of the Daityas, Yakṣas, and Asuras danced;
thereafter, the earth, the refuge of various people, [was covered] by hundreds of millions [of them].
Adorned with islands, mountains, rivers, oceans, and the circle of treasures,
[the world consists of] Jambū, Śāka, Kuśa, Krauñca, Śālmalī, Gomeda, and Puṣkara.
The continents are double the size of [Jambudvīpa], starting from one hundred thousand [yojanas], and are surrounded by oceans beginning with the Salt Ocean;
beyond that is the golden earth and the Lokāloka mountain.
Beyond that darkness lies the Garbhoda ocean and the shell of the world-egg; this is the surface of the earth, adorned with the Triśaila mountains, rivers, continents, and the oceans of fire.
O Śakra, Lord of the Gods, you who perceive everything directly, I wish to hear in detail about the divine Earth while you are speaking. (MṛgT 1.13.38)
My mind, drawn irresistibly by the certainty of what has been declared, runs toward the sacred revelation;
O best of the twice-born, I shall proceed, embodying the discourse already set forth.
Listen with a one-pointed mind to [the description of] the continents, rivers, and forest borders:
Jambūdvīpa is the navel of the earth; it is circular and measures one hundred thousand yojanas.
It is surrounded by the salt ocean, which in turn is surrounded by [the mountain range] of equal extent;
situated in its center is the golden king of mountains, the monarch of peaks.
Mount Meru, frequented by the gods, eclipses the light of the sun;
it extends sixteen thousand [yojanas] from the surface of the earth down into the ground.
That [pillar], being sixteen units wide at its base,
increases by four units at each of its three joints, reaching one hundred thousand units in height.
The rims, shaped like bracelets, protrude and are exceedingly radiant;
one is ten thousand [yojanas] high, while the other is eleven thousand.
The rim near the edge of the summit, which is the refuge of the world-protectors and possesses the radiance of all jewels, they call the Cakravāṭa.
Below that, on the joints [of the mountain], dwell the Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Mahās; and on the eastern and other directions reside Indra and the others. Learn their names from me. MṛgT 1.13.46.
Adorned with circles of light-nets from various jewels,
frequented by Siddhas, Sādhyas, and Maruts, Amarāvatī is the golden ground of Hari.
Tejovatī belongs to Vahni; it abounds in red and yellow jewels, with golden ramparts and gate-towers, and is inhabited by beings equal to fire.
The city of Saṃyamanī belongs to Death; it is encircled by high walls of iron and is inhabited by the messengers of the Pretas, such as Kāla, Pāśa, and Pitṛvya.
The dark river, frequented by the Daityas, was like the abode of Death, the lord of the Daityas;
it was adorned with a magnificent canopy formed by the spreading net of light from blue jewels.
Constructed from crystal stones, the palace of the Lord of Waters at Śuddhavatī shines with abodes resembling white clouds, frequented by aquatic creatures.
The city of Vāyu, however, is fragrant, filled with lofty white and yellow banners,
inhabited by powerful beings, and constructed from all kinds of jewels.
The great city of Mahodayā, white with pearls and other precious materials,
shines, praised by throngs of twice-born brahmins, with palaces that possess the luster of the snowy mountains.
The city Yaśovatī, born of all jewels and served by Rudra, bears the fame of having consumed Smara and Death with the blazing eye on its forehead.
Thus, these eight cities, which provide comfort in all seasons, extend across half the Cakravāḍa range; they are reddened by the pollen of the Pārijāta trees shaken by the wind.
"Created by the Ordainer for the welfare of those who follow the wheel of the world-protectors, heaven is thus celebrated on earth by poets. (MṛgT 1.13.56)
In the center of the self-existent [world-system] are fourteen thousand yojanas; there lies the city named Manovatī, which is venerated by the lords of the world.
With the splendor of its light, it rose high above the paths of lightning, making them ruddy;
as if vying with the goddess Sāvitrī, it surpassed even those who long for heaven.
In that [city], the gods and sages of great luster worship the Lord of Great Yoga, the creator of beings, for the sake of perfection, through the observances beginning with restraint (yama).
In the northeastern quarter of that mountain is a peak resembling the sun;
they call it Jyotiṣka, which is eternally dear to Paśupati.
Upon its golden ridges, variegated with jewels,
are stationed the foremost hosts of attendants, beginning with Skanda, Nandin, Mahākāla, and Gaṇeśa.
At the summit is the abode of the God of gods, the enemy of Tripura,
frequented by tens of thousands of Rudras and the supreme deities headed by Brahmā.
Thus, below Meru and at its edge, there are mountains situated in the cardinal directions;
learn from me now the nine regions (*varṣa*) remaining within this [continent] of nine islands. *MṛgT* 1.13.63.
Niṣadha, Hemakūṭa, and Himavat are the best of mountains;
to the south of Meru is Nīla, and to the north are Śveta and Śṛṅgin.
Extending two thousand [yojanas] in width, ten in height, and nine in the intervals between them,
these mountains of the gods stretch toward the east, their peaks resting upon the ocean.
To half that extent, Mālyavat and Gandhamādana extend as their diameter;
situated to the south and north of Meru, they are at the same distance from it toward the east and west.
To the east of Mount Mālyavat and to the west of Mount Gandhamādana lies Ilāvṛta; it extends south of Mount Nīla and north of Mount Niṣadha.
To the east of Mount Mālyavat lies the region of Bhadrāśva, filled with auspicious people;
and to the west of Mount Gandhamādana lies Ketumāla, also known as Suketana.
To the south of Niṣadha and to the north of Hemakūṭa lies Harivarṣa;
to the south of Himavat is the region known by the name Kimpuruṣa, which is Bhārata.
To the north of Nīla is the region called Ramyaka; to the north of Śveta Mountain is Hiraṇya;
and that which lies north of Śṛṅgavat is called the Kuru-varṣa.
For the stability of Meru, the Creator fashioned four mountain-pillars rising fifty thousand [yojanas]; among them, Mandara is situated to the east.
Śveta, resembling the color of turmeric powder, is to the south; Gandhamādana is to the west;
Vipula and Nīla are to the north; and Supārśva is to the east, being reddish in hue.
Within those [continents] stand the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpadruma), casting a shadow of a thousand yojanas;
these are the Kadamba, Jambu, Aśvattha, and Nyagrodha, located at the northern borders.
The river produced from the juice of jambū fruits, having circled Mount Meru,
entered its very base, turning that earth into gold.
Having drunk that, birds, serpents, mice, wild animals, monkeys, and other creatures—
whatever beings bathed in it— became golden.
Although there were other wish-fulfilling trees on the continents, Jambu became their "island-banner" (dvīpaketu);
because of its preeminent power, this [continent] is therefore known as Jambūdvīpa.
At the foot of the Viṣkambha mountain in the east is the Caitraratha forest;
there is a lake named Aruṇodaka, adorned with golden lotuses.
At the foot of the southern mountain, surrounded by Gandharvas, Suras, Siddhas, and Apsarases, lies the Nandana grove; there is the Mānasa lake, which steals away the mind.
At the base of Vaipula is the Vaibhrāja mountain, and there is the Sitoda, the best of lakes;
it is frequented by the gods and covered with lotuses possessing the brilliance of sunbeams.
On Mount Saupārśva is the forest named Dhṛtimat and the auspicious lake Bhadraka,
covered with fragrant lotuses, which is always frequented by the ancestors.
In the continent surrounded by the Sutvagitā mountain, people have a lifespan of thirteen thousand years, subsist on the juice of jambu fruits, and perceive objects through the light of Mount Meru.
In Ketumāla, people have a lifespan of ten thousand years, possess the luster of a blue lotus, subsist on the essence of the jackfruit tree,
and are happy and strong, endowed with divine bodies.
In Bhadravājinī, one who feeds on blue lotuses possesses the luster of the moon's orb;
with a lifespan of ten thousand years, he is abandoned by suffering, grief, and fear.

In the Kuru region, the lifespan is thirty thousand years; people subsist on the fruits of the wish-fulfilling trees, give birth to twins, and possess a complexion like the luster of dark-blue flowers.
Two thousand *bhūta*-vedas are marked by the junctions in each direction;
they are frequented by Siddhas, Munis, and Cāraṇas, and are the abodes of Soma and Vāyu.
The two continents are Candrabhadra and Ākarau; their inhabitants have the complexion of the moon and the red lotus.
Their lifespan is that of Ailāvṛta, and their food consists of fruits and roots.
Their inclusion within the ocean is proclaimed due to their proximity;
therefore, the lifespan in Hiraṇvatī is twelve thousand five hundred years.
In Ramyaka, there is a twelvefold duration for people who constantly eat lakuca fruit and possess the splendor of blue lotuses like the moonlight.

O Ikṣvāku, possessing the luster of silver, for as many thousands of years as it takes a person eating the fruit of the banyan tree to pass away, for that long does a person live when Hari is present.
Raukma is in Kiṃpuruṣa, where the inhabitants eat from the Plakṣa tree and live for ten thousand years;
thus have those regions beginning with Kiṃpuruṣa been described to you.
There is no difference in their states among those who evolve as creators and so forth;
they possess wisdom, lifespan, splendor, strength, wealth, and progeny in accordance with the respective ages.
In Bhārata, people eat what is ploughed and unploughed, afflicted by the three kinds of suffering;
yet there is one virtue: that if they apply themselves, they can accomplish anything they desire.
Since the land of action (*karmabhūmi*) is the cause for all lands of fruition (*phalabhūmi*),
there are nine islands here in the current of the ocean, and nine in the region of half-land.
Learn from me their names, beginning with Indradvīpa:
Indradvīpa, Kaśeru, Tāmraparṇa, and Gabhastimān.
Nāgadvīpa, Cāndramasa, Gāndharva, Vāruṇa,
and the ninth, called Kumārika, as well as various mountains and rivers.
In the land of Bhārata, which is proclaimed to be filled with people of various castes,
there was a king named Āgnīdhra, the lord of Jambūdvīpa, born in the lineage of Manu.

The [oceans] beginning with Bhārata are designated by names derived from their respective kings, [and they are filled] with waters that have the essence of salt, milk, curd, fat, juice, honey, and nectar. (MṛgT 1.13.97)
The continents, beginning with Jambūdvīpa, are doubled in size starting from one hundred thousand [yojanas], and they are surrounded [by oceans].
In Śāka[dvīpa], there is a Śāka tree, O dear one, which is the basis for the name "Śāka."
Kuśa was born as Kāñcana in the lineage of Kauśa when Svayambhū desired to perform a sacrifice;
meanwhile, the Daitya Krauñca was slain on the Krauñca mountain in a golden cave.
Having fought for a very long time with Skanda, who was full of wondrous illusions,
that mountain became famous because of the deeds of that Daitya, Citra.
Because it attained the state of being a peak (ketu) by its name, it is called Krauñca;
in Śālmala there is a Śālmali tree, made of gold, a thousand yojanas high, and radiant as the sun.
Beloved by the immortals, that banner of theirs was bound to his name;
in Gomeda, there was a king named Gopati, who was intent upon the Gosava sacrifice.
He became the sacrificial priest for those of the lineage of Manu, the Autathyas, who were like fire;
when they had set out to perform sacrifices to Hari, he [approached] the Bhṛgus as his gurus.
Out of anger, Gautama cursed him so that he went to destruction within ten steps;
those cows of his were burnt by the sage’s fire of wrath in the sacrificial enclosure.
The earth was covered with its fat, and from that it became the Gomeda [region];
there is a river named Puṣkariṇī, adorned with golden lotuses.
By her, that Puṣkaradvīpa was made known as being frequented by gods,
just as people have always made their dwellings among the Kimpuruṣas and others.
Likewise, in Śākadvīpa and the other continents, his food consists of milk and similar substances;
he possesses the luster of snow, the moon, frost, the blue lotus, grain, and crystal.
The lifespan is ten thousand years; with suffering destroyed, there is but a single thorn.
Within the seventh ocean, there are two crores and three-quarters of a *dala*.
And fifty thousand [yojanas] from the ear, which contains a golden mountain within it,
there is a golden ground with various jewel-trees and mountains.
Ten crores of worlds were created by the Creator for the sake of sport for the gods;
beyond that is the Lokāloka mountain, which regulates the light and darkness of those worlds.
With a diameter of ten thousand yojanas and adorned with lofty peaks,
the light of the sun upon its summits resembles the radiance of the moon.
O Sage, because it is drawn away [by the sun], it does not heat the abodes of those who dwell in the quarters;
beyond that is dense darkness for nineteen hundred thousand yojanas.
Forty thousand, thirty-five crores,
twenty-seven lakhs, and one crore [of beings] emerged from the ocean.
A golden basin, ten million [yojanas] in extent, extends all around from the interior;
the Bhuvarloka, measuring one hundred and fifty thousand [yojanas], reaches as far as the pole star from the surface of the earth.
In the *KSTS* edition it reads *dhruve prānto*,
but it is quoted in the commentary on *Svacchanda-tantra* 10:516c–517b as *dhruvaprānto*.

The world of the gods (Svarloka), which has its boundary at Dhruva and is the refuge of the foremost among the celestial beings, is ten million times smaller than that [Brahmaloka]. (Svarloka according to KSTS).
But it is quoted up to the end of this *pāda* in Svacchanda Tantra 10:516c–517b,
which implies that this word-split was indeed made:
*mahardvikoṭiryatrāste marīcyādimunivrajaḥ //* (Mṛgendratantra 1.13.115)
The people there are distinguished by their eighty-fold [virtues], taking refuge in the ancestors and Jahnu; there dwells the great yogi Sanandana, who is like ten million suns in his ascetic heat.
R̥bhu, Sanatkumāra, and Sanaka of great austerity—
beyond that is the abode of Truth, Satyaloka, belonging to the Self-Existent One (Svayambhū).
Endowed with an abundance of desire, nine and seven crores [of beings] dwell there,
where Sāvitrī stands in embodied form and the Vedas abide along with their followers.
Then there are four and six [worlds] belonging to Madhu and Tripuravidviṣ (Viṣṇu), located respectively in Jyotiṣmatī and Citrā; and [beyond them] is the Koṭi-egg-shell.
"Extending over a hundred crores" refers to the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍagolaka);
in terms of measurement, this [egg] is essentially equal across all streams [of worlds].
Śakra protects its eastern direction; Agni protects the southeastern;
the Destroyer of Beings (Yama) protects the southern; and the Rākṣasa protects the southwestern.
The god Varuṇa [presides over] the western direction; Nabhasvān, the northwestern;
Soma and Yakṣeśa, the northern; and Īśa, the northeastern direction.
Above is Brahmā and below is Hari, who are always intent upon all matters;
even over these, ten Rudras stand as controllers, ten for each.
Even those who possess the earth do not step beyond their place out of fear of these beings,
who possess various forms, great heroism, and a radiance equal to the rising sun.
They are surrounded by those bearing various weapons; learn their names from me:
Budhna, Vajraśarīra, Aja, Kapālīśa, and Pramardana.
The Teacher, the wielder of the Pināka bow, and the lord of the thirty gods are synonymous with Prāgvibhūti, Avyaya,
Bhasma, Kṣaya, Antaka, Hara, Jvalana, Agni, and Hutāśana.
Piṅgala, Khādaka, Babhru, and Dahanā reside in the direction of Agni;
Vidhātṛ, Dhātṛ, Kartrīśa, Kāla, and Viyojaka [reside in the other directions].
Yama, Dharmeśa, Saṃyoktṛ, and Hara are the leaders of Yama;
while Nirṛti, Māraṇa, Krodha, Hantṛ, Dhūmra, and Vilohita [are the leaders] of Nirṛti.
The deities of the Palāda class are Ūrdhvaliṅgin, Virūpākṣa, Daṃṣṭrin, Bhīma,
Balapāśa, Atibalapāśa, Aṅga, Śveta, Bhūta, and Jalāntaka.
The Kapas possess great strength and long arms, and their roars sound like the thundering of clouds;
they are swift, rapid, and of great velocity, yet subtle, sharp, and bringers of destruction and end.
Kapardin, Abdeśa, Pañcānta, Pañcacūḍa, and Vāyupa;
Nidhīśa, Rūpavān, Dhanya, Saumya, and Śāntajaṭādhara.
The lords of the moon and the yakṣas are the illuminators of the splendor of the grace of desire;
they are the masters of the sciences, the possessors of all knowledge, the knowers of the Vedas, and those who have reached the supreme Veda.
Vidya, Vidhatṛ, Bhūteśa, Balipriya, Sukhādhipa, Śambhu, Gaṇādhyakṣa, Vibhu, Tryakṣa, and Caṇḍāmara—the praised ones. (MṛgT 1.13.133)
And [the lords] Vicakṣaṇa, Nabholipsu, Saṃvivāha, Mūrdhan,
Krodhana, Anilabhuk, Bhogin, Grasana, Udumbara, and Īśvara.
Vṛṣa, Viṣadhara, Ananta, Vajra, Daṃṣṭrin, and Viṣṇupāda;
from them arise the regions of enjoyment beginning with Ambhas, which are situated within those [worlds].
The five groups of eight [disciples] who were appointed as instructors, possessing the glory of the fruit obtained from their fields [of activity],
were Bhārabhūti, Āṣāḍhi, Ḍiṇḍi, Lākulya, and Amarapuṣkara.
Prabhāsa and Naimiṣa—this is the group of eight secret sites in the water;
as well as Śrīśāla, Jalpa, Kedāra, Bhairava, and Āmrātakeśvara.
Hariścandra, Mahākāla, Adhyā, Sātipada, Ruci,
Mahendra, Bhīma, Vimala, Kurukṣetra, Gayā, and Khalā.
In the [region of] Khaga, there are Sanāpadottara, Sāṭṭahāsa,
Sanākhaḷa, Sthāṇu, Svarṇākṣa, Gokarṇa, Bhadrakarṇa, and Mahālaya.
Ten million Rudras called Vastra, Pada, Vimukha, and Aha [dwell] in the circle of the sky;
these they call the eight purifiers (pavitrāṣṭaka) within the sphere of pride, the elements, and the senses.
O best of the twice-born, I shall tell you the names of the eight Sthāṇus:
Mākoṭa, Maṇḍaleśāna, Dviraṇḍa, and Chagalāṇḍaka.
Sthūla, Sthūleśvara, Śaṅku, Karṇa, and Kālañjara, as well as the eight subtle cities of the gods; among these, the Paiśāca realm is at the beginning in the intellect (buddhi). 1,13.142.
The Rākṣasa, Yākṣa, Gāndharva, and the highly powerful Māhendra;
the Saumya, Prājeśvara, and Brāhma—blazing with supreme splendor.

In the secondary sense, the abodes of the Lord of Yogins are those established by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Kumāra, Umā, and finally Śrīkaṇṭha; [these are] the uncreated and the created, beginning with Raibhava and ending with Bhairava.
The radiant splendor of Vīrabhadra, praised by the best of yogins,
[shines] beneath his own feet, possessing a glory superior to all Rudras established in their respective offices.
Vāmadeva, Bhava, Ananta, Bhīma, Īśvara, Tatpuruṣa, Sarveśāna, Īśāna, Eka-vīra, and he who is known as Eka-śiva. MṛgT 1.13.146.
Fierce and with a formidable gaze, the lords are established at the summit of all qualities;
having worshipped through intense austerity, they are considered to have attained mastery over anger and other passions.
The Rudras, who possess all-encompassing vision and action, are sharp in their own respective offices;
hear now of the lords of the Pradhānas, who possess ten times the glory of them.
Krodheśa, Caṇḍasaṃvarta, Jyotiḥpiṅgala, Sūra,
Pañcāntaka, Ekavīra, and Śikheda— these are remembered as such.
He possesses all the senses, all bodies, and is the substratum of all internal organs;
he is the driver within the Puruṣa and Niyati, and at the proper time, he possesses the power of differentiation.
Bhuvaneśa, Mahādeva, Vāmadeva, Bhava, Udbhava, Ekapiṅga, Ekeṣaṇa, Īśāna, and Aṅguṣṭhamātra—these are radiant. MṛgT 1.13.151.
Resembling the Supreme Lord, they are the lords of the mandala within the sixty-four great cities of the mandala, situated at the stage of *kalā* within the womb of *rāga* and *vidyā*.
The infinite protector of the three times, the lord of security, the master of Brahman,
the two Rudras who are the abode of firm splendor, the Lord of the Deep, and the sovereign of the universe.
The Rudras who preside over *māyā* are the lords of the mandalas;
they cause the multitude of beings mounted upon the wheel of saṃsāra to revolve.
This entire ground of existence for all beings is indeed so terrible;
therein the ignorant sink down like immobile cows in the mud.
Bhṛguṇī, Brahmavetālī, Sthāṇumatī, Ambikā, Parā, Rūpiṇī, Nandinī, Jvālā, and Saptasaptārbudeśvarā—these are the [goddesses]. 1,13.156.
The Vidyārājñīs, praised by Rudra, are said to reside within the Vidyā;
above them stands the radiant and glorious Lord, the Sovereign of Vidyās.
Accompanied by the eightfold assembly of Rudras pervaded by the consciousness of the Lord of Mantras,
they are Ucchuṣmas, Śambaras, Caṇḍas, and those of great heroism who strike down their enemies.
The Rudras, the Gaṇas, along with the guardians of the directions (dikpālas), the Śāstras, and then the Lords (patayas)—
those beginning with Ananta— have indeed been declared by name.
O Brahmin, those very forms of his own nature previously arose through the sequence of questions;
in the state of Sādāśiva, he is accompanied by the limbs of purification (pavitrāṅga) and the entire retinue beginning with the Sakala.
Lord Sadāśiva resides in the Bindu; the lords of the Kalās, beginning with Nivṛtti, reside in the Nāda;
and the Lord of Sound (Dhvanipati), the best among all possessors of power, resides in the Śakti.
The womb of the universe is Vāgīśā; beyond her are the Lords, ending with Sadāśiva and Śiva, wherein the existence of the individual soul (aṇu) is fashioned as the path (adhvan).
The repose of all transcendence occurs beyond that; how could there be lords above it?
Having transcended Īśāna, the principle up to the end of Śānta is known as Sādāśiva.
Even the worlds, the *nāda* and other *kalās*, and no lord other than Śiva [exist];
rather, whatever distinction of lords exists within this [system] is like the distinction of powers (*śakti*) described in the scripture.
Through the metaphorical application of the distinction between functions, that [distinction] arises from the difference in the locus of those [functions];
by means of which powers he brings about the unfolding of human energy.
She is the sovereign of the worlds known as Nivṛtti and the others;
that power by which she causes beings to turn back is her "Nivartikā" (the one who turns back).
"Nivṛtti" is that station; the Lord there is also possessed of cessation (nivṛtti).
It is the path by which one who has ceased [from worldly activity] returns again, being unlike the previous state.
That installation (pratiṣṭhā) is negated, as well as its location and its presiding deity;
for by means of that [installation], one bestows knowledge upon the individual soul (aṇu), having abandoned the sphere of objects accessible to the authoritative means of knowledge.
That is the Vidyā, and its locus is also [the body]; its Lord is Vidyeśa, by whom Hara effects the pacification of all her sufferings.
That is peace and that is the supreme state; by practicing that, one also becomes possessed of peace.
Furthermore, there is the great and even greater illumination of the objects above and below.
And those [energies] by which the supreme consciousness is made great and one is liberated—
namely Indhikā and the others— their locus is that [state], and Īśa exists within all three.
