Even though [the soul] possesses qualities such as omniscience, that [power] by which it wipes away its state of being subject to injunctions—even in part—due to impurity, is its liberator; and that is its true state.
The *mocaka* (liberator) is the one who performs that action by which he brings about Īśāna;
he is the upward-moving one (*ūrdhvaga*) and his station is that [of Īśāna], and thus he is the Lord of the upward-moving ones (*ūrdhvagāpati*).
Even those who have attained that state through the yoga of Śaiva practice,
having experienced the joy that lasts until the end of that state, proceed to the supreme state.
"And they do not perform creation and so forth, because they are intent upon their own self-interest;
thus has the principle of Sadāśiva been briefly explained for you. (MṛgT 1.13.175)
The same applies even in the case of Śakti; thus, this [deity] is "with parts" (sakala) through connection with ritual action (kṛtya).
That ritual action has the [deity] beginning with that [Śakti] as its object, while elsewhere it is always "without parts" (niṣkala).
O Sage, in the knots (*granthi*) predominant in the various stages (*bhūmi*), and in the *vidyā*, *bindu*, *kalā*, and so forth,
the multipliers (*guṇakāra*) beginning with ten occur below the tip of the *nāda*.
Above Kalā is Vidyā, and below it are heard the lords of the Gahana; the notion that "the interval between them is this much" is merely indicative of the intellect (dhī). MṛgT 1.13.178.
In this manner, for both paths characterized by sequential production,
there is a dissolution in reverse order, extending as far as the two principles of Śakti.
O Blessed One, you who perceive all things, tell me: how and to what extent is there the dissolution of both the individual and the collective [aspects] of the path to reality? MṛgT 1.13.180.

During the Great Sleep (mahāsvāpa), there is the intermediate dissolution (avāntara-laya) of everything both collectively and individually; likewise, the time of persistence (sthiti) and creation (sarga)—as they are being described—should be understood. 1,13.181.
A day for the one born from the golden egg (Brahmā) lasts for a thousand cycles of four yugas; his night is of equal duration.
By this measure of day and night, he reaches the end of half a parārdha of years.
This dissolution occurs in reverse order, beginning from *prakṛti* and so forth;
at that time, the hundred Rudras and the two heroes, Śrīkaṇṭha and [Ananta], are the lords of *pradhāna*.

Having pervaded the subtle universe and the subtle bodies endowed with consciousness by means of its power, [the Lord] attends to Time, which dwells within the latent impressions situated in primordial nature (prakṛti), until the end of that sleep.
Impelled by the one who bears the mantra beloved of Śiva, and urged by the lords of the mandalas,
they bring forth the world at the proper time and carry out their respective offices.
Karma, dharma, and so forth are considered qualities residing within the intellect;
since a quality does not depart from its possessor, how can it be said that they reside in primordial matter (prakṛti)?
Truth is indeed a quality of the intellect; a quality does not depart from that which possesses it.
However, because [truth] resides within the body, the senses, the fruits [of action], and the levels of existence, it is figuratively attributed to them.

The wise have declared that indication (lakṣaṇā) occurs in the case of a substratum, a cause, an effect, that which is proximate, a benefactor, and in the imitation of qualities such as dharma. (MṛgT 1.13.188)
Thus, at the end of a parārdha of the creations of the qualities and so forth, Māyā, turning away from her own office, devours the kalā that is the cause of the qualities.
Upon its cessation, the gods who hold office therein also cease;
for their authority over creation, maintenance, and so forth, is dependent upon that [office].
Thus, among the twenty principal lords of mantras, the one who has attained the desired state always consumes the Vidyā-tattva; that is the Bindu, the sound of the Bindu.
The supreme Śakti consumes the sound (nāda), while Hara himself rules over that Śakti;
thus, for the repose of living beings, Śiva is beyond even Māyā.
Having perceived [the world] through the power of its own vision, it proceeds toward creation;
in this manner, the principles (tattvas), entities (bhāvas), worlds (bhuvanās), and bodies (vapus) [come into being].
O Brahmin, the pure and impure paths have been briefly explained;
[the principles are] Vidyā, the five bodies of atoms, Bindu, Nāda, and then Kāraṇa.
The five aggregates are the supreme path; where do existents abide as conditions?
There is the subtle sound, the digit, time, passion, and the pair, together with the Person.
O Sage, the gross sound (nāda) consists of five kalās and rests upon the five principles;
the bindu consists of four kalās and is the repository of the four knots beginning with Pradhāna.
In pride (garva) reside the gods headed by Manomukha; in intellect (buddhi) reside Bhāva and the others.
The god whose body consists of the five mantras resides in the five subtle elements (tanmātra); the lords of mantra and the mantras themselves are established in the gross elements.

Thus, that abundant net of bonds consisting of the unseen (adṛṣṭa), the seeds of darkness, and so forth—which obstructs the subtle [soul] and is perceived by those whose vision follows the paths of the Paśu-mata—is the Śāmbhavī perfection of mantra; its power remains unimpeded as it shines forth through the ritual action to be described for the purpose of pacifying that [net].
And the Vidyāpāda is completed.
